title: Vertical Farming
desc: Plan and run a small indoor or stacked farm: crops, light, water, nutrients, climate, food safety and business case.
outcomes: Explain how stacked growing works and what suits it.
Set light, water and nutrient schedules.
Compute yield, energy and water per kilogram.
task: Plan and run a small stacked growing pilot with schedules, logs, hygiene plan, harvest records and unit economics.
condition: A small space or shelving kit, lights, seeds, a spreadsheet, two peers and a grower mentor.
standard: Schedules are followed and logged; yield per tray recorded; hygiene plan applied; energy and water per kg calculated; cost per kg shown; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Growers, hospitality staff, school teachers, urban entrepreneurs.
evidence: plan, daily log, harvest record, cost sheet
modules: Choosing crops that pay
Understand
Start with the crop and the buyer, not with the equipment.
Fast, light, high-value crops suit stacked growing: microgreens, lettuce, herbs, edible flowers and some strawberries.
Cycle times: microgreens 8 to 12 days, lettuce 30 to 40 days, herbs 4 to 6 weeks.
Ask three local buyers what they buy weekly, at what price and in what pack.
Rank crops by income per tray per week.
Three buyers want 20 kg of basil per week at 300 INR per kg. A basil tray gives 1.2 kg every 5 weeks, so about 85 trays in rotation are needed.
Make a demand table with three buyers, quantities and prices and choose three crops.
Choice is supported by buyer numbers and cycle times.
Growing systems and fail-safes
Understand
Choose a system you can run reliably.
Deep-water culture floats plants on aerated nutrient solution; nutrient film technique sends a thin stream over roots; ebb and flow floods and drains trays.
Aeroponics saves the most water but fails fastest if a pump stops.
Plan for failure: a battery or generator for pumps, alarms, and a manual watering routine.
Keep a spare pump and tubing.
A 4-level ebb-and-flow rack uses a 40 L reservoir and a timer. When the pump fails at night, a battery alarm wakes the grower within 10 minutes and the crop survives.
Draw your layout and write a fail-safe plan.
Layout labels parts; plan covers power and pump failure.
Light schedules and cost
Apply
Light is usually the largest running cost.
Intensity is measured as photosynthetic photon flux density; many leafy greens do well at 150 to 250 micromoles per square metre per second.
White full-spectrum LEDs work for most beginners.
Hang lights 20 to 40 cm above the canopy and raise as plants grow.
Use timers; 12 to 16 hours of light a day for most leafy crops.
A 4-tray rack with 100 W of LEDs for 14 hours uses 1.4 kWh a day. At 8 INR per kWh, that is 11.2 INR per day for the rack.
Set a light schedule and calculate daily light energy cost.
Schedule and cost are correct and recorded.
Water and nutrients
Apply
Plants take nutrients dissolved in water, so water quality is crop quality.
Measure pH (about 5.8 to 6.2 for lettuce) and conductivity (about 1.2 to 1.8 mS per cm) every day.
Add nutrients slowly and test again after 30 minutes.
Change the solution on a schedule and keep it covered from light to prevent algae.
Never mix concentrated nutrients together before dilution.
A reading of pH 7.2 is corrected with a few millilitres of acid solution, then re-tested after 30 minutes and logged.
Keep a 14-day reading sheet.
Log has daily pH, conductivity, temperature and actions.
Climate, hygiene and food safety
Evaluate
Indoor air is warm and humid, which is ideal for disease.
Keep humidity near 50 to 70 per cent and airflow gentle but constant.
Wash hands, clean tools, use a footbath or shoe change and quarantine new plants.
Remove diseased plants at once; sanitise trays between cycles.
Wash and pack produce in a clean area; keep a harvest record.
Grey mould appears at 85 per cent humidity. A small fan and a dehumidifier bring humidity to 65 per cent within a day and the outbreak stops.
Write a hygiene and cleaning schedule.
Schedule has daily, weekly and between-crop tasks.
Yield, energy and water
Analyse
Measure efficiency to compare crops and decide what to scale.
Yield per square metre of floor area counts all levels.
Water use is often much lower than field growing; energy per kg is the weak point.
Track weight per tray, losses and sales.
Compare cycles to find improvements.
A 6 m2 floor with 4 levels gives 24 m2 of growing area and produces 40 kg of lettuce every 5 weeks, about 8 kg per week at 9 kWh per kg.
Calculate yield, energy and water per kg for your pilot.
Calculations are correct with units.
Unit economics and break-even
Evaluate
A viable unit needs steady sales.
Cost lines: racks, lights, pumps, space rent, power, water, seeds, nutrients, labour, packing and transport.
Sell direct to restaurants and shops, and consider weekly subscription boxes.
Break-even kilograms per week = weekly cost / margin per kg.
Test price and yield changes.

Weekly costs of 9,500 INR and a margin of 110 INR per kg give break-even of about 86 kg a week. The unit grows about 8 kg a week (40 kg every 5 weeks), so it needs either more levels, a higher price or lower costs.
Build a weekly break-even sheet.
Break-even is calculated and compared with output.
Ninety-day pilot and decision
Create
Run long enough to see repeats.
Set weekly targets for yield, losses and energy.
Log every problem and fix.
Hold a review at day 30, 60 and 90.
At day 90 decide: scale, change crop or stop.
By week 12 the pilot sells 62 kg of herbs, loses 6 per cent to disease and cuts energy per kg by 12 per cent after lights are moved closer.
Write the day-90 decision memo.
Memo uses real numbers and a clear decision.
quiz: Which crops suit?
Leafy greens, herbs, microgreens. (Covered in module 1: Choosing crops that pay. To pass that module: Choice is supported by buyer numbers and cycle times.)
Why LEDs?
Efficient, less heat. (Covered in module 3: Light schedules and cost. To pass that module: Schedule and cost are correct and recorded.)
What pH range?
About 5.8 to 6.2 for many crops. (Covered in module 4: Water and nutrients. To pass that module: Log has daily pH, conductivity, temperature and actions.)
Why hygiene?
Prevent disease. (Covered in module 5: Climate, hygiene and food safety. To pass that module: Schedule has daily, weekly and between-crop tasks.)
Yield measure?
Per m2 per cycle. (Covered in module 6: Yield, energy and water. To pass that module: Calculations are correct with units.)
Energy per kg unit?
kWh per kg. (Covered in module 6: Yield, energy and water. To pass that module: Calculations are correct with units.)
Biggest risk?
Pump or power failure. (Covered in module 2: Growing systems and fail-safes. To pass that module: Layout labels parts; plan covers power and pump failure.)
Why compare to field?
See whether it pays. (Covered in module 6: Yield, energy and water. To pass that module: Calculations are correct with units.)
What is break-even?
Volume covering costs. (Covered in module 7: Unit economics and break-even. To pass that module: Break-even is calculated and compared with output.)
Why log readings?
Spot trends. (Covered in module 4: Water and nutrients. To pass that module: Log has daily pH, conductivity, temperature and actions.)
rubric: Daily light, water and temperature recorded
Log used to explain one crop loss or gain
Food-safety, water and electrical rules for the place are written down
Rules checked with the authority and a hazard plan tested
